opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I find really exciting, partly because it's one of the places where smell is so different from vision or hearing. When you see a color, there's not much emotional baggage attached by default. But when you smell something, the hedonic response, whether it's pleasant or unpleasant, whether you want to approach it or avoid it, is almost the first thing your brain computes. Pleasantness is arguably the most dominant axis of human odor perception. So if you build a good map of odor space, valence isn't a separate thing you bolt on afterward. It's woven into the geometry.

The way I think about it, the embedding we learn from molecular structure captures perceptual similarity: things that smell alike sit near each other. The natural next step is to ask whether there are directions in that space that line up with how people feel about smells. You can collect ratings of pleasantness, comfort, disgust, arousal, and see how well a simple model on top of the embedding predicts them. If a linear readout works well, that tells you emotion is fairly accessible from the representation, which is a nice validation that the map is capturing something real about how humans experience smell.

The important caveat is that valence has an innate component and a learned component, and they're tangled together. Some responses look fairly universal, like aversion to the smell of rot, which makes evolutionary sense. Others are deeply cultural and personal. A smell that's comforting to one person because it reminds them of their grandmother's kitchen might be neutral or off-putting to someone else. Wintergreen is a classic example: in some places it reads as candy, and in others it reads as medicine. So I don't think you get a single valence score per molecule. You want a shared map of odor space, and then a layer for individual and cultural context on top of it, something closer to personalization than a universal label.

That's also where I think the applications get meaningful. If you understand which regions of odor space tend to evoke calm, or alertness, or nostalgia, you can start designing with intention, whether for wellbeing, for consumer products, or for people who've lost their sense of smell and are trying to recover that emotional dimension of life. Losing smell is underappreciated as a quality-of-life issue, and a lot of what people report missing is exactly this emotional texture.

So my short answer is that the perceptual map comes first, because you need a coordinate system. Then emotion becomes a set of functions over that map, some shared across people and some shaped by memory and culture. Untangling those two is one of the most interesting open problems in the field.

r001.rationale: It says the embedding captures perceptual similarity, with odors that smell alike sitting near each other.

r002.rationale: It proposes predicting emotion ratings from a layer on top of the odor map, rather than jointly embedding emotional valences and olfactory information.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because smell is kind of the odd one out among the senses in this respect. With vision, you can look at a scene and describe it pretty neutrally. With smell, that's almost impossible. The first thing people say about an odor is whether they like it or not. Pleasantness is the dominant axis of how humans describe smells, and that's not an accident of language. It's wired in. The olfactory bulb projects more or less directly into the amygdala and the limbic system, so emotional processing is happening before you've even consciously registered what you're smelling.

So when we built the principal odor map, we were initially just asking: can a model predict what a molecule smells like from its structure? Does it smell like rose, does it smell like garlic, and so on. But once you have an embedding space that captures that, valence kind of falls out of it. Pleasantness turns out to be one of the major axes of variation in the map. Molecules that people rate as pleasant cluster in one region, unpleasant ones in another, and that's learned from the data, not something we imposed.

The way I think about connecting those two things has a few layers. The first is purely descriptive. If you can predict hedonic tone from structure, you've got a tool that perfumers and flavor chemists have never really had, which is a way to search chemical space for things that will feel a certain way before anyone synthesizes them.

The second layer is more interesting to me scientifically. A lot of what we call valence in smell is probably about the stimulus carrying information about the world. Things that smell bad tend to be things that are bad for you: decay, spoilage, microbial activity. Things that smell good often signal nutrients or ripeness. So I suspect the embedding is partly capturing a kind of evolutionary prior. And there's evidence that the pleasantness axis correlates with fairly simple physical properties of molecules, like molecular weight and how compact they are. Which means the emotional response is not arbitrary. It's a readout of chemistry.

And then the third layer is the one we're furthest from, which is going beyond pleasant and unpleasant into richer emotional states. Calm, alertness, nostalgia, comfort. Those are real, people experience them, but they're much harder to measure. Nostalgia in particular is almost entirely about individual history, so no molecular model is going to predict that from structure alone. You'd need to combine the odor embedding with something about the person.

That's actually where I think the field has to go. The map gives you a representation of the stimulus. To get to emotion, you need to pair it with physiological measurement, so heart rate, skin conductance, maybe neural recordings, and with behavioral data at scale. Then you can start learning the mapping from odor space to affective space, rather than relying on people to introspect and label how they feel, which is notoriously unreliable.

The long-term vision, honestly, is that smell becomes something you can design with the same intentionality as sound or color. Right now it's a craft practiced by a small number of very talented people working largely by intuition. If we can make the relationship between molecules and feelings legible, that opens it up enormously.

r001.rationale: The response says the embedding captures odor descriptions and that pleasant and unpleasant molecules cluster separately, but it does not state that proximity in the map represents similarity in perceived smell.

r002.rationale: The response proposes pairing the odor representation with physiological and behavioral data to learn a mapping to affective space. It does not propose jointly embedding emotional valences and olfactory information.

astra-6.text:
I think of that as learning a mapping between two spaces. On one side, you have an olfactory embedding—a representation of what something smells like. On the other, you have a person’s emotional response: Is it pleasant? Is it calming? Does it evoke a particular memory?

To connect those, you need people to smell things and describe their responses. Then you can ask which parts of that relationship generalize across people and which are personal. The same smell might be comforting to you because it reminds you of your grandmother’s kitchen, and mean something completely different to me.

So I wouldn’t expect emotional valence to be a single label attached to a molecule. I’d envision a model that takes the odor representation, but also something about the person and the context, and predicts a range of possible responses. The interesting question is how much we can learn from the shared structure before we need that individual history.

r001.rationale: It describes an olfactory embedding as a representation of what something smells like, but does not say that proximity in the map represents similarity in perceived smell.

r002.rationale: It proposes mapping between olfactory and emotional-response spaces, but does not propose jointly embedding emotional valences and olfactory information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two pieces to that. One is learning a representation of odor—an embedding where molecules that smell similar end up near one another. The other is understanding how that representation relates to a person’s experience: Is this pleasant? Is it calming? Does it evoke a particular memory?

I wouldn’t assume there’s a single emotional label attached to each point in that space. Some responses may be shared across people, but others depend on your history and the context. The same smell might remind one person of home and another person of something unpleasant.

So I’d approach it by collecting those responses alongside the odor descriptions and asking how much we can predict from the embedding, and how much requires knowing something about the individual. That gives us a way to connect the chemistry to emotion without treating emotion as simply a property of the molecule.

r001.rationale: It says molecules that smell similar end up near one another in the odor embedding.

r002.rationale: It proposes collecting emotional responses alongside odor descriptions and relating them to the embedding, but does not propose jointly embedding emotional valences and olfactory information.
